title: Small Context Units
one_liner: Keep change-relevant code cohesive and navigable; treat excessive size as a signal to inspect, not an automatic failure.
problem: A large file or class can mix unrelated reasons to change and make the relevant dependency set hard to find. Physical size alone does not establish this: a long cohesive unit may be easier to work with than many short files joined by hidden coupling. Fixed line and method caps can reward mechanical fragmentation.
solution: Use file, class and function size as local review signals. For representative changes, inspect responsibilities, dependency closure, callers, tests and the code an agent actually needs to read. Extract a cohesive unit behind a clear interface when that reduces unrelated context or change risk; keep cohesive code together when splitting would add indirection. Calibrate any lint threshold to the language, generated-code status and observed outcomes. Evaluate correctness, navigation effort and review cost rather than treating a universal line count as an LLM capacity limit.

model_guidance.task: Changes involving a large file or class
model_guidance.evidence: Long-context code studies identify task and position effects but do not validate a fixed file-size cap for compact models.
model_guidance.note: Use scoped search and tests; extract only when the boundary reduces change-relevant dependencies.

model_guidance.task: Changes involving a large file or class
model_guidance.evidence: LongCodeBench found that longer files were not consistently associated with worse repository QA accuracy.
model_guidance.note: Measure the model–harness pair and workflow before enforcing a size budget.

model_guidance.task: Tool-using agent works in a large repository
model_guidance.evidence: Modern coding agents can navigate large file-system corpora with tools; no direct controlled file-split benefit was established.
model_guidance.note: Keep a cohesive module intact unless extraction improves testability or change locality.
